headlines.article_text: Some in Florida and Alabama without power as Isaias moves north Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Copper Brock helps salvage what he can from the Milton Quick Stop after the roof was torn off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on Oct 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with Category 2 winds. Joe Raedle | Getty Images News | Getty Images Nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power early Sunday as remnants of Isaias moved north, where widespread moderate to heavy rainfall was expected across the central Appalachians and mid-Atlantic region. Heavy rainfall was expected to be the "primary hazard" as the storm moves north, said Philippe Papin, a senior hurricane specialist at the National Hurricane Center in Miami. Parts of the southeastern U.S. and mid-Atlantic could see scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts, according to the National Weather Service. "We're expecting that heavy rainfall to continue here across the central Appalachians into the mid-Atlantic here during the day on Sunday, and we're still expecting isolated flash and urban flooding, and there may be also some residual gusty winds associated with the system as it continues to kind of move up the spine of the Appalachian mountains," Papin said. At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians. Isaias made landfall Friday as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. Despite warnings of storm surges, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak Saturday and free of the downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes. Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city's mayor said the airport "took some damage." The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of a high-rise facade in Panama City Beach. A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building's insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about. In Florida's Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home, and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man's family members, ranging in age from 4 to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said. Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city's fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state's emergency management agency. Along Alabama's Gulf Coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines. President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after earlier doing the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid. The U.S. Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation's strategic petroleum reserve to address storm-related supply disruptions. The National Weather Service said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods. Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon was a Category 4 storm with 150 mph (241 kph) winds as it approached Mexico's coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern Mexico beginning Sunday, with life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Saul Loeb | AFP | Getty Images The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the White House television press pool's decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law, an agency spokesperson said Saturday. Emily Covington, a department spokesperson, said group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law. "The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws," she said. The announcement came after the television pool of five broadcasters ceased presidential coverage last month after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Late Saturday, messages were sent to the five outlets seeking comment: ABC, CBS, CNN, FOX and NBC. The White House press pool, a rotating cast of news outlets that cover the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over whether the president, or anyone, can control the content of news reports—a type of free speech and a pillar of American democracy. Last month's developments marked an extraordinary escalation in Trump's efforts to restrict news reporters and outlets that he finds insufficiently supportive. CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued over the days-long ban. A judge lifted the ban after granting the three news organizations a reprieve, which is in place until Tuesday. Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists' regional director for the Americas, criticized the administration's decision to investigate on Saturday.
